newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Ambitious warlords wreck fragile Tajik peace.
newsitem.headline: Ambitious warlords wreck fragile Tajik peace.

text.p: Robber barons flouting the authority of a weak government are tipping the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan back into chaos only months after a deal to end a four-year civil war.
President Imomali Rakhmonov on Sunday blamed a flare-up of violence on rival warlords and crime barons battling for supremacy.

Clashes which flared in the capital Dushanbe on Saturday followed a steady slide into anarchy during Rakhmonov's 10 years in office and a four-year civil war which a peace deal, signed last June, is supposed to have ended.

"The people who provoke these military clashes are connected with the economic mafia, the drugs mafia and the criminal world," Rakhmonov was quoted as saying in a statement issued after his Security Council met.

When Rakhmonov and his Islamist foes signed a peace agreement in June intended to end the civil war, many of Tajikistan's 5.7 million people feared new bloodshed would be provoked by the return of armed guerrillas to Dushanbe.
But it was squabbling warlords nominally loyal to Rakhmonov who sparked the new violence and one man, maverick commander Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, may be poised to take advantage.
The politically ambitious Khudoyberdyev, 34, commands an elite government armoured brigade and has long been viewed by Western diplomats as a potential coup-maker.

Russian news agencies said Khudoyberdyev's forces were fighting troops belonging to Rakhmonov's presidential guard south of Dushanbe on Saturday and Sunday. He was quoted as threatening to move tanks into the capital.

But the fighting which erupted on Saturday with tanks, mortars and rockets, had humble beginnings -- a revenge attack for the death of an uncle of Sukhrob Kasimov, the commander of a unit of Interior Ministry troops.
Kasimov seized a northern district of Dushanbe on Sunday and fighting died down there.
Underlying Kasimov's quarrel with Yakub Salimov, a customs chief and former interior minister, is a battle for turf.
In the last decade, Afghan-style paramilitary groups have carved up the remote, mountainous republic bordering Afghanistan and China into a confusing patchwork of fiefdoms.
"If you want to understand Tajikistan," said a seasoned Western diplomat, "you have to take yourself back to mediaeval Europe. You have here a very weak king and a lot of powerful robber-barons."
The "robber-barons" fight for control of the few riches the republic has to offer -- a declining cotton crop, aluminium, gold and drugs.
"There's been a complete breakdown in law and order," said a Western aid worker speaking on condition of anonymity. "There's too many heavily-armed people wandering around."

Rakhmonov's administration has been shown to be impotent in two previous mutinies, both by Khudoyberdyev. He might now feel powerful enough to defy an ultimatum by Rakhmonov's Security Council to stop fighting within three days.

One factor which might make Khudoyberdyev pause for thought is the presence in Tajikistan of 20,000 Russian troops carrying out peace-keeping duties and guarding Tajikistan's frontiers. They are widely regarded as Rakhmonov's guarantors.
The peacekeepers, under the auspices of the Commonwealth of Independent States, whose mandate ran out last month, threw up only a few lightly-armed checkpoints around the city centre.
"The Russians are at a loss," said a diplomat. "They understand fighting between the government and the Islamists but the fighting inside the government foxes them."
"With its drubbing (against separatists) in Chechnya only just behind it, the Kremlin is unlikely to want to wade into a war in far-flung Central Asia."
As gunmen stalk the city, Dushanbe's inhabitants can only sit and wait nervously in their homes to see if the warlords back down or if the fighting leads to longer-term violence.
